concept.name: Fair value gap
concept.definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a three-candle pattern in which the middle candle's range does not overlap with the wicks of its neighbors — the low of the third candle sits above the high of the first (bullish FVG), or the high of the third sits below the low of the first (bearish FVG) — leaving a span price crossed in a single fast pass. It is read as an inefficiency that price may later revisit; that expectation is a hypothesis, not an established regularity.
concept.intuition: The middle candle moved so fast that a slice of prices was skipped; the gap marks the skipped slice.
concept.mechanics: Scan consecutive three-candle sequences: for a bullish FVG, check whether candle 3's low exceeds candle 1's high — the gap is the void between them. Traders mark the span (sometimes refined to its midpoint, the 'consequent encroachment') and watch for a retracement into it as entry context, with invalidation beyond the gap's far edge.
concept.formula: Bullish FVG exists when Low(candle3) > High(candle1); gap span = [High(candle1), Low(candle3)]. Bearish FVG exists when High(candle3) < Low(candle1); span = [High(candle3), Low(candle1)].
concept.failure_modes: FVGs are extremely common, especially on low timeframes, so most carry no information; many are never filled, and 'price returns to balance inefficiencies' is an untested slogan rather than a documented tendency.
concept.misconceptions: That an FVG must be filled; unlike session gaps (where 'gap fill' at least has a mechanical definition), there is no validated fill-rate for FVGs, and the concept repackages older notions of price vacuums.
concept.example: Candle 1 tops at 100.20, candle 2 surges to close at 102, and candle 3 bottoms at 101.50: the 100.20-101.50 span is a bullish fair value gap watched for support on a retrace.
